title: Fed's Waller Puts a Rate Hike Back on the Table, Invoking the Ghost of 2021's 'Transitory' Call
summary: Fed Governor Christopher Waller warned this week that the central bank may need to raise rates if upcoming inflation data runs hot, explicitly framing the choice around not repeating the Fed's 2021 error of dismissing inflation as transitory for too long. The remarks matter less for the specific probability they imply than for what they reveal about a Fed leadership under Kevin Warsh that has stripped away forward guidance, leaving the rates path to swing on individual speeches and data prints rather than a settled committee view.
context:
- Warsh's decision at his first meeting as chair in June to drop explicit forward guidance was framed as preserving flexibility; Waller's comments this week show that flexibility currently being used to keep tightening, not easing, live as an option — a reversal of what markets had assumed a change in Fed leadership would mean.

- Waller's framing deliberately invoked the Fed's 2021 mistake of calling inflation 'transitory' and waiting too long to act, then immediately hedged that 'the desire to avoid past mistakes is often the author of new ones' — a rare public airing of the internal debate over whether the Fed is now at risk of overcorrecting for its last error.

- The trigger is conditional rather than settled: Waller tied the case for a near-term hike specifically to that week's CPI and PPI releases, illustrating how reactive the rates outlook has become to single data points under a Fed that no longer telegraphs its reaction function in advance.

- This marks a further hawkish shift from the picture painted by June's FOMC minutes, which had already pushed the market's expected first rate cut out to 2027; Waller's remarks go a step further by putting a hike, not just a longer pause, back into the realistic range of outcomes ahead of the 28-29 July meeting.

- Treasury yields moved higher on the remarks, underscoring that bond markets are now pricing meaningful two-way risk around the July decision rather than treating a hold as the only plausible outcome — a marked change from the cutting-cycle narrative that dominated market expectations for most of the year.

title: AI Chip Stocks Tumble Into a Bear Market as Wall Street Questions Who Actually Needs All This Compute
summary: The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell sharply this week, dropping close to a quarter from its late-June high and meeting the technical definition of a bear market, as investors reassessed whether hyperscalers' AI capital spending will generate matching returns. The sell-off matters as the first real stress test of the AI trade's central assumption — that demand for compute is effectively unlimited — after chip stocks had more than doubled over the preceding twelve months on exactly that premise.
context:
- The scale of the reversal is only legible against the scale of the preceding rally: the semiconductor index had climbed roughly 130% over the prior year, meaning this week's slide is best read as a partial unwind of a valuation built almost entirely on the expectation of continued hyperscaler spending, not a reaction to a single disappointing print.

- A specific catalyst was reporting that Meta plans to launch a unit reselling surplus AI training and inference capacity; if a hyperscaler has spare compute to sell rather than an unmet need to fill, that undercuts the scarcity assumption underpinning chip demand forecasts.

- SK Hynix's decision to delay expansion of next-generation HBM4 memory in favour of higher-margin, more conventional DDR5 production was read by investors as a supply-side confirmation from within the chip industry itself that AI-linked memory demand growth may be moderating, rather than accelerating as capex guidance had implied.

- The damage was broad rather than confined to one name: Micron's memory-focused business, Intel's foundry and legacy PC exposure, and AMD's position as the main alternative GPU supplier all fell sharply, indicating the repricing is about the AI capex cycle generally rather than one company's execution.

- The timing compounds the risk: this is the first serious test of high-multiple AI growth stocks under a Fed that has just signalled hikes are back in play, since a higher-for-longer or rising rate path leaves far less room for the valuation expansion that carried chip stocks through the prior year's rally.

title: Record Wall Street Profits Arrive Alongside Confirmation That AI Has Already Cut a Third of Some Bank Jobs
summary: JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs and rivals reported record second-quarter profits this week, powered by a surge in trading and dealmaking activity, even as JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon disclosed that AI has already eliminated 30 to 40% of headcount in some divisions. The juxtaposition matters because it offers one of the clearest real-world data points yet on how AI is reshaping a major industry's workforce — while Dimon's own caution that this isn't making the bank 'dramatically cheaper' to run complicates the simple narrative that AI automatically converts into fatter margins.
context:
- The record results were driven substantially by trading revenue and one-off windfalls, including fees Goldman Sachs earned advising on the SpaceX IPO, tying bank profitability directly to the same market volatility — from the Iran-linked oil spike to the chip sell-off and shifting Fed expectations — that has unsettled other parts of the market this year.

- Dimon's disclosure that AI has already cut staffing by 30-40% in specific units, with most affected employees redeployed rather than simply let go, is one of the most concrete admissions yet from a major employer about AI's present-tense effect on headcount, as opposed to the more speculative framing common in most corporate AI commentary.

- Dimon pushed back on the assumption that these cuts translate into a leaner cost base, arguing competitive pressure is channelling most of the efficiency gains through to customers rather than to the bank's own margins — a point that complicates the simple 'AI equals lower costs equals higher profits' narrative many investors have been pricing into AI-adopting companies.

- The scale behind the disclosure is significant in its own right: JPMorgan now runs close to 1,000 AI use cases against an annual technology budget of roughly $20 billion, with token-processing costs still 'immaterial' but expected to grow substantially through the second half of the year.

- The combination of record bank profits and confirmed AI-driven job losses is likely to feed into the broader debate the Fed is already having about whether a resilient headline economy can coexist with a quietly softening labour market, since banks are typically viewed as a bellwether for the health of the wider corporate sector.
